newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan to adopt new law on minority Ainu.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan to adopt new law on minority Ainu.

text.p: Japan is set to scrap a century-old law that academics and activists say has long served to discriminate against Japan's indigenous Ainu people.
But the Ainu, whose population is now concentrated in Hokkaido, the northernmost and second largest of Japan's four main islands, are not giving the new law wholehearted welcome.

The law, expected to be enacted later this a year, would set up a fund to study Ainu culture. But Ainu activists say it does not go far enough in restoring the culture and rights they have lost to mainland Japanese over the centuries.

"If the new law is just the first step toward raising living standards of the Ainu, we welcome it," said Michiaki Okada, a Japanese married to an Ainu woman in Shiraoi, a small Hokkaido town of 23,800 people where 1,000 Ainu live.
Okada teaches the Ainu language in this southern Hokkaido town that, through exhibitions of Ainu culture, tries to ensure the Ainu way of life continues.

The Ainu, along with other ethnic minorities such as Japan-born Koreans and Chinese, and "burakumin", a hereditary member of an "untouchable" caste, have always suffered varying degrees of unequal treatment, especially in the past century.

A recent Hokkaido prefectural government survey shows there have been improvements in Ainu standards of living, but many still cannot afford higher education for their children after compulsory education ends.
The average income of an Ainu in Hokkaido was 3.02 million yen in 1993, compared with 5.55 million yen for the average Hokkaido resident.
LIVING STANDARDS NEED TO BE RAISED
"I wonder if the new law is going to divert people's attention to the culture of Ainu people and away from the core of the problem, raising their standard of living," Okada said.
The survey shows that about 17 percent of Ainu polled either had faced or had heard about derogatory treatment at school or the work place.
The Ainu, who also once inhabited the northern tip of Japan's largest island of Honshu and the Russian island of Sakhalin, are now largely assimilated with the Japanese.
Their abundant hair, broad, flat faces and deep-set eyes do not always physically distinguish them from other Japanese.
Official data show there are about 25,000 Ainu in Hokkaido. But Ainu activists say there may be twice that number because many Ainu are reluctant to disclose their roots.
Some activitists say there may be another 10,000 Ainu outside Hokkaido. Many left to escape discrimination. No nationwide survey has been conducted on the number of Ainu.
Scholars say there are traces of Ainu habitation of Hokkaido dating back 10,000 years.
In the late 1800s, an influx of Japanese settlers on Hokkaido pushed the Ainu into small pockets of the island, depriving them of their unique culture and land.
In 1899, a law called "Former Hokkkaido Natives Protection Law" was enacted to assimilate them into Japanese society.
EVEN FOOD RIGHTS ERODED

Shigeru Kayano, Japan's first and only Ainu member of the Upper House of parliament, claims the 1899 law was used to suppress the Ainu and erode rights such as restricting them to a tiny quota of salmon, the Ainu's staple food.
"Not many minority races in the world have been deprived of their staple food," Kayano said. The new legislation replacing the 1899 law is expected to be enacted this year.
It has been tentatively named "the Law To Promote Culture and Understanding of the Ainu."
Kayano said the act should be renamed the "Law To Promote Culture and Living, and Understanding of the Ainu Race."
"For the Ainu, the new law is not satisfactory. But it's better than nothing as it took nearly 50 years to have the 1899 law replaced," he said of the struggle to have the act changed.
Ainu activists have called for a new law since the end of the Second World War.
The proposed new law is not expected to fully recognize the Ainu as an aboriginal race -- a main pillar of their demands.
It is likely to recognise the "indigenous nature" of Ainu people, but allow no special rights by Ainu to claim or seek the return of land expropriated over the centuries.

The new law calls for a comprehensive study of the Ainu, the establishement of a fund to preserve and promote Ainu culture including language, and the promotion of understanding about Ainu through education.
Ainu outside Hokkaido do not welcome the new legislation as it is unlikely to apply to Ainu living outside the island.

"We find nothing to appreciate in the legislation. No Ainu has been invited to participate in drafting of the new law," said Takao Yokoyama, a member of an Ainu association in Tokyo where about 2,700 live.
